I am pleased to introduce this money laundering risk assessment for the banking sector in the Isle of Man. The Financial Crime Strategic Board (FCSB) would like to thank the Isle of Man Bankers' Association for its assistance in conducting this risk assessment and in particular, representatives from the sector who participated in the Banking Working Group.
In recent years the banking sector has actively participated in several thematic reviews that the Isle of Man Financial Services Authority (FSA) has undertaken and published, and this National Risk Assessment comprehensively builds upon the previous 2020 money laundering and terrorist financing risk assessment. The FCSB recommends that the sector reviews the findings of this assessment, and ensures that, where required, identified actions are adopted into business, customer and technology risk assessments as appropriate.
Banking is central to our Island economy and fundamental to the safe and effective operation of both domestic and international businesses established here. The FCSB therefore also urges other financial sectors and designated businesses to read this report and where relevant review their own activities accordingly . An overall National Risk Assessment for money laundering (with a summary of the key findings of this report) and National Risk Assessments for terrorist financing and proliferation financing, will also be published.

body:
This executive summary presents the principal findings from the Isle of Man's latest Banking sector Money Laundering Risk Assessment, aligning with the broader National Risk Assessment framework and building on the 2020 ML/ TF NRA.
Undertaking an NRA is a core requirement of the FATF, the international body responsible for setting and reviewing global standards for anti-money laundering, countering the financing of terrorism and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction (AML/CFT/CPF). The FATF 40 Recommendations provide the international standards which all countries are expected to meet; it is IOM Government policy to adhere closely to these recommendations. The focus of this report is on ML risks, with separate assessments planned or published for Legal Persons and Arrangements, Virtual Assets, Terrorist Financing, Non-Profit Organisations, and Proliferation Financing. A horizontal Executive Summary is planned once all NRAs are complete.
2.1 The Isle of Man's banking sector serves both domestic and international customers, with banking forming a critical component of the Island's financial system and economy. The sector is largely comprised of branches or subsidiaries of major UK and international banks and is fully regulated by the FSA.

chunk_id: Banking Sector National Risk Assessment (October 2025), 2. Executive Summary - 555dc71365ca1bea
body:
2.2 KEY HIGHLIGHTS FROM THE ASSESSMENT INCLUDE:
- Sector Size and Activity: The sector employs approximately 2,000 people and holds over £40billion in deposits, processing nearly £80billion in annual payments. Banking represents 7.6% of the Island's national income, third only to insurance (17%) and online gambling (13.6%).
- International Profile: The Isle of Man is an international finance centre, and the majority of business - by value and number of clients - is international in nature, especially with strong connections to the UK and South Africa. This international profile increases the sector's exposure to crossborder money laundering threats, particularly the risk of foreign proceeds of crime entering the financial system.
- Risk Assessment: Using the World Bank methodology, the overall risk of ML to the sector is assessed as mediumhigh. The risk level is a product of the medium-high threat facing the banking sector, and a medium residual vulnerability to ML (i.e. after considering mitigating controls). Inherent vulnerabilities remain in products and services with international features, rapid transaction capabilities, exposure to foreign politically exposed persons (PEPs), use of cash, and level of robustness of technological controls. This overall banking risk level has increased from medium since the 2020 NRA and is a product of an increasing threat landscape, rather than a reduction in the banking sector controls.

body:
- Vulnerable Segments: The most vulnerable segments are international deposit services and certain corporate/trust services, each with high inherent vulnerability scores. However, final vulnerability is reduced following application of AML controls.
- Trends and Emerging Risks: The banking sector has seen an increase in Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) from 2021 to 2024, largely driven by international threats such as fraud, tax evasion, organised crime, and the use of virtual assets as well as increasing awareness in the sector of the requirement for SAR reporting. There is also a rising threat from Asian and UK-based organised crime groups and the increasing pace and complexity in financial flows. This is reflected in ongoing investigations, including in relation to online gambling and cyber enabled crime.
- Supervisory and Legal Framework: The Isle of Man maintains a comprehensive legal and supervisory structure, and recent regulatory enhancements have targeted areas such as business introducers, PEPs, and targeted financial sanctions risk management. Ongoing risk-based supervision, thematic reviews and enforcement actions continue to strengthen AML/CFT/CPF systems and controls.

The banking sector ML risk assessment identifies a small number of areas for improvement; these are aligned to the strategic aims from the National Financial Crime Strategy 2024-2026. The actions are outlined in Section 11 of this report and summarised below.
- As part of embedding the operation of the IOMFCP for the banking sector, a programme of preparing and publishing typologies based on actual cases should continue to be expanded. This will assist the sector to continue to improve, learn and develop and maintain a robust control environment.
- To continue to help protect customers of banks in the IOM, relevant stakeholders (banks, the FSA, FIU, other Government agencies) should continue to develop workstreams to help reduce fraud risks, not only from the ML perspective, but more generally. The IOMFCP is expected to play a role in this work.
- The FSA should continue to work with banks on ensuring the data it receives is of good quality and accurate, and if necessary, provide further guidance for banks.
- Taking into account the supervisory structure within the FSA, and improvements in data systems and analytical capability that has been implemented, policies and procedures should be put in place to document how the data is used and analysed, how frequently reports are produced and their scope and content, and to which parties such reporting is made (including outside the FSA, for example to the FIU, banks, and IOMFCP).

3.3 As with most IFCs, previous NRAs have highlighted that the services provided in the IOM may be used to conceal the proceeds of crime or to conceal or disguise the origins of those proceeds, through international transfers of funds and the use of complex corporate structures. headers: 8. Actions identified in the 2020 ML/TF National Risk Assessment
body:
8.1 The 2020 NRA assessed the Banking sector as posing a medium overall risk for money laundering. The inherent risk associated with domestic retail customers, including high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs), was rated as medium. However, the involvement of international retail clients (including HNWIs), corporate clients, and trust-related structures was assessed to carry a medium-high inherent risk due to their complexity, cross-border nature, and potential opacity.
8.2 Given the need to keep requirements up-to-date and make continuous improvements, there have been some enhancements and revisions to the framework since the 2020 NRA, although there were no Banking sector-specific recommended actions arising. One of the revisions of particular relevance to banks was the implementation of the updated "Introduced Business" paragraph within the AML/CFT Code 2019 ("the Code").
8.3 This new paragraph mandated that, when a customer is introduced by one entity (the introducer) to another (such as a bank), and elements of customer due diligence (CDD) are provided by the introducer, the bank must assess the risk associated with the introducer as part of the broader customer risk assessment. This assessment should also consider internal mitigation factors, such as whether the customer has been met by staff of the receiving entity and the way CDD was obtained by the introducer.

8.4 Risk-based supervision of banks for AML/CFT/CPF has been ongoing for a long time and has continued to strengthen since the 2020 NRA. Specific work has been undertaken to evaluate the scope of risks faced by banks in the IOM. For example, the FSA undertook a thematic exercise between 2021 and 2023 to assess the AML/CFT/CPF preventative measures and controls that firms (including banks) apply in respect of foreign PEPs. This review identified areas where further improvements were needed in some banks to better demonstrate compliance with the Code requirements. Where appropriate, civil penalties were imposed to address deficiencies and reinforce regulatory expectations.
8.5 More recently, targeted work examining banks' systems and controls for managing sanctions risks has been undertaken. Thematic feedback was issued by the FSA in May 2025 and highlighted several positive outcomes. All inspected entities provided documented procedures and controls to manage sanctions risk, with most showing effective escalation and transaction monitoring processes. The FSA also noted thorough staff training programmes.

9.1 The overall ML threat to banks has been assessed as being medium-high, consistent with the overarching national threat assessment, noting that there is a medium domestic threat, but a medium-high international (cross-border) threat.

9.2 The ML threats to the Banking sector derive from persons/ entities who wish to abuse the system to launder the proceeds of crime. In the IOM, it is generally considered that the ML threats are greater than the TF threat, and this is evidenced from SAR reporting by banks, and from requests to banks from law enforcement. The TF NRA reports that the number of TF-related SARs submitted by banks was extremely low and that the banks had no recent enquiries referred to them of potential TF from the authorities. There was only 1 internal TF disclosure in 2022 and 1 in 2023, compared to 9 internal sanctions disclosures in 2023 and over 1,000 internal money laundering disclosures for the same period.

body:
- 9.3.1 As an IFC, the IOM's Banking sector primarily serves non-resident clients. This cross-border profile means that funds often originate outside the jurisdiction, and related predicate offences typically occur overseas. This increases the risk of foreign criminal proceeds entering the domestic banking system, with detection and verification made more difficult by geographic and legal distance.
- 9.3.2 The IOM's broad range of financial services and competitive tax regime, like those of other IFCs, may be exposed to misuse by individuals seeking to conceal the proceeds of crime, due to the international and often non-face-to-face nature of its business, along with the complexity and speed of transactions and availability of specialised professional services.
- 9.3.3 The exception is drug trafficking and supply, where the use of IOM banknotes paid into third-party accounts and subsequently transferred to the UK remains a common laundering method. While this typology has persisted over time, there is no clear evidence of a significant increase in threats to the Banking sector from this activity in recent years.
- 9.3.4 The IOM's primary ML threat, however, continues to be the use of the financial system for the placement and layering of funds from predicate offences committed overseas. Financial flows often involve rapid cross-border transactions and the misuse of third-party accounts, both individual and corporate.

- 9.4.1 There has been an increase in the number of active international money laundering cases under investigation, with 10 during 2024-25. The PIMLIT, supported by the wider IOM Constabulary (IOMC), has conducted three major multi-agency operations this year, with assistance from other Isle of Man agencies. The cases are complex, with multi-jurisdictional structuring (including shell companies) and a range of financial products used to hide criminal proceeds. The Island's economic growth in other sectors, as OCGs also seek to grow, has created risks to which the Banking sector has been exposed. Organised immigration crime (including human trafficking) and transnational organised crime centred on sophisticated large-scale, cyber-enabled fraud and integration of funds associated with online gambling, predominantly Asian-facing, are providing new challenges. The increased level of reporting from banks concerning fraud and organised crime reflects the growing global trend identified in several international reports, including a report by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) in April 2025, which highlights actions taken in the IOM targeting an online gaming company in connection with a fraud and money laundering investigation.

Comprehensiveness of the AML Legal Framework 0.8 Very High
A comprehensive legal framework and updated sector-specific guidance from the FSA and FIU are in place. The fully regulated banking sector is supervised by the FSA for AML/CFT/CPF and prudential matters. Since the 2016 MONEYVAL assessment, the legislative and policy environment has remained stable. Most IOM banks belong to larger groups that must meet standards set by multiple jurisdictions, which may differ from local requirements. There is effective cooperation and ongoing dialogue between the banking sector and IOM authorities.
Effectiveness of Supervision Procedures & Practices 0.8 Very High
The FSA is responsible for consumer protection, reducing financial crime, and maintaining sector confidence through regulation. Its inspection and supervisory methods are publicly available and guided by internal policies and governance frameworks.
Over the past seven years, the FSA has gathered AML/CFT annual returns and financial flow data from banks. This data contributes to a risk-based supervision approach and sector reports that are made available on the FSA website. The use of technology solutions has facilitated risk analysis and the production of sectoral and entity-specific risk heat maps. Since 2023, the FSA has expanded its technical and human resources for AML/CFT/CPF policy work and inspections, with ongoing training for staff to support inspection processes.

By analysing sector reports and AML/CFT returns, the FSA identifies Banking sector risks and uses these insights to guide supervisory planning and resource allocation.
The FSA consults with banks' internal audit and compliance teams and the Isle of Man Bankers' Association, supporting anti-financial crime initiatives through ongoing partnership, consultation, and participation in initiatives led by the Isle of Man Financial Crime Partnership.
Availability and Enforcement of Administrative Sanctions 0.8 Very High
A comprehensive range of regulatory measures (enforcement and supervision) is available, including civil penalties, public statements, action against individuals (e.g. prohibition), directing firms to take action (including remediation), and utilising third party reporting professionals, as well as measures like licence suspension or revocation. Key regulations introduced in 2015 and 2019 have enabled the use of administrative actions and financial penalties to address breaches in the financial sector.
Decisions on discretionary civil penalties follow established internal governance procedures, including the published Enforcement Decision-Making Process. The FSA has published a Guidance Note explaining the discretionary civil penalty framework.

When a sanction is imposed, the relevant entity must implement a remediation plan, which will be subject to monitoring and verification as necessary. There are publicly available examples demonstrating the application of civil penalties, highlighting enforcement actions taken against financial institutions including banks and DNFBPs. These are accompanied by public statements regarding the contraventions involved. Since 2020, four civil penalties have been issued against four banks, amounting to £2,978,251 (£2,084,776 after discounts reflecting agreed settlements and remediations). Public statements have been released in relation to each case.
According to an Island Global Research survey of industry participants, 91% of respondents indicated they were aware or very aware of these enforcement actions, illustrating the effectiveness of such measures as a deterrent.
Availability and Enforcement of Criminal Sanctions 0.6 Medium High
A comprehensive range of criminal sanctions is available. Individuals who contravene the Code are guilty of an offence, with the courts empowered to impose both custodial and financial penalties at levels intended to serve as a suitable deterrent. Offences under POCA include failure to report a suspicion as well as "tipping-off."

The framework governing criminal sanctions is robust and thorough. Currently, there have been no instances of criminal sanctions applied within the Banking sector; accordingly, this control has been assessed as Medium High rather than Very High. This rating reflects the generally high levels of compliance observed in the sector and the effectiveness of the civil penalties regime which have so far negated the need for criminal sanctions.
Availability and Effectiveness of Entry Controls 0.8 Very High
Entry requirements for the Banking sector are very high. The FSA's Licensing Policy outlines the specific criteria that applicants must meet to obtain and retain a financial services licence for deposit taking.
Authorisation decisions are made by the CEO or Head of Division of the FSA, with input from relevant senior managers and divisions as needed.
A licence is only issued if the FSA determines that the applicant, including associated individuals, meets the fit and proper requirements to perform regulated activities.
The fit and proper test is applied both at the initial licensing stage and on an ongoing basis during regulated activity. This assessment includes considerations of integrity (including criminal history), financial standing, and competence.
The FSA maintains case studies of both successful licence applications and instances where applications were not pursued, including related to deposit taking.

Integrity of Banks' Staff 0.8 Very High
The general level of integrity and the operating environment in the IOM is very high. There are strong entry controls in place. Banking is a mature sector; there is often group oversight and a range of policies in place for dealing with staff issues. Staff in specified roles (controlled functions) are subject to a fit and proper test undertaken by the FSA.
Domestic corruption or bribery is not identified as a concern in the IOM. Cases of staff fraud or theft are infrequent, and banks are required to notify the FSA of any matters that may lead to serious disciplinary action being taken against a member of staff; this includes instances where criminal prosecution of a bank employee or controlled function role-holder occurs.
The FSA collects data on notifications concerning fraud, staff discipline, criminal convictions, and employee screening, which may affect assessments of individuals' fitness and propriety. As noted above, the FSA must also be informed of certain disciplinary actions and can prohibit individuals from working in the sector or in particular roles when necessary.

Core banking practices include robust recruitment processes, performance management, implementation of the "three lines of defence" model (risk management, compliance, audit), a robust policy framework, and continuing professional development requirements including ethics and integrity. Regulated businesses are advised to assess their own risks when applying the framework. Annual AML/CFT training is mandatory for all banking staff, and directors have specific continuing professional development (CPD) requirements. Resources from organisations like the World Bank, FATF, and MONEYVAL are also used, alongside in-house training. The use of technology and AI for training has grown, boosting staff AML knowledge. POCA requires that banks report all suspicious transactions - actual or attempted, regardless of the amount. This includes AML/CFT/CPF suspicions under POCA and the Anti-Terrorism and Crime Act 2003 (ATCA). It is an offence not to do so. Section 24 of the FIU Act 2016 allows banks to report matters that may assist the FIU but are not seen as ML/TF matters.
There is a well-established reporting framework in place. There is also a requirement for ongoing monitoring of customers and transactions in order to identify suspicious transactions. Banks have well embedded and sophisticated systems in place, using automated transaction monitoring systems with transactional records for AML screening, monitoring, and reporting as well as PEP screening. The FIU inform the FSA of any known issues with banks' reporting (including quality of SARs and their timeliness) and permits the FSA to raise any concerns with banks (through agreed handling conditions). If there are persistent issues, the FSA may undertake a targeted inspection or use this information as part of wider inspection planning. The FIU provides guidance documents as well as feedback to MLROs on SARs submitted. Banks will audit the process themselves through all three lines of defence. The MLROs, who have access to the bank boards, will also flag any issues. The main area of learning continues to be around "request for consent." The IOMFCP has been doing work with banks and TCSPs on a consent training product. However, the quality of feedback score for banks is already very high.
Banks have consistently been one of the largest reporters by sector, and the number of SARs from banks has been steadily increasing since 2020 (noting a levelling off in 2024). The number and generally good quality of reports help to indicate a strong effectiveness in monitoring and reporting. Data from the annual AML/CFT returns to the FSA covers internal and external banking SARs and demonstrates that the sector can effectively identify unusual and suspicious activity and has clear procedures to escalate via the correct channels; the conversion rate of internal disclosures to external was on average 44% in the last 3 years (2022-2024).

Level of Market Pressure to Meet AML Standards 0.8 Very High
AML oversight by external international bodies (e.g. MONEYVAL) and the involvement of the Banking industry in the NRA and international assessments assists understanding of the jurisdictional risks of non-compliance with international AML standards. The government also seeks to educate and inform the sector on risks.
There is ongoing pressure to meet AML requirements, including international Wolfsberg standards for correspondent banking, especially since banks are often part of global groups held to high compliance expectations. Local bank leaders recognise that non-compliance can cause significant reputational damage, business loss, and licensing threats. The industry believes much of this compliance pressure comes from internal ethics rather than correspondent relationships. Banking groups closely monitor compliance risks through strict governance, reporting, and regular internal audits. Correspondent banks use transaction monitoring systems to detect suspicious or sanction-violating activities.

The AML/CFT/CPF regulatory framework requires banks to collect details of the beneficial ownership of their customers and verify this information. Information about the beneficial ownership of companies and trusts, including those domiciled in the IOM, can be obtained by the bank either directly from the customer or through an authorised introducer, such as a TCSP. If specific criteria are met, including ongoing testing and monitoring by banks, it is permissible for a bank to rely on the introducer to retain the verification documents related to the beneficial owner.
Access to beneficial ownership information contained in company registers varies by country, as does the quality of the information. In December 2024, the IOM made its register accessible to banks and other obliged entities. The Banking sector states that while the IOM register helps confirm existing information or detect changes, it is not used for verification.
The FSA monitors compliance with the Beneficial
Ownership Act 2017 (BOA) and evaluates whether relevant persons fulfil their BOA obligations. Details on FSA oversight of the BOA are available here; banks are unlikely to be subject to beneficial ownership inspections.

chunk_id: Banking Sector National Risk Assessment (October 2025), Banking Typologies - 3e3b22c011f4dc9a
body:
- Typology: Disguised Proceeds as Business Revenue; Scenario Summary: An Isle of Man company (Company X) opens a bank account, claiming profits stem from its TCSP operations abroad. Within six months, the bank observes unusually high transaction volumes for a new business. Investigation uncovered that the company is under scrutiny in another jurisdiction for money laundering services to organised crime groups.; Key Risk Indicators: ●High volume of funds for new business ●Cross-border company structure ●Links to jurisdictions with known financial crime risk
- Typology: Bribery and Corruption; Scenario Summary: Application for a transactional account by a foreign national, director and partial owner of a company from a country with low Corruption Perceptions Index score. Adverse media reveals past bribes; individual in a senior role at the time. Application declined and reported.; Key Risk Indicators: ●Applicant from high-risk country ●Negative media/SEC Order ●Connection to historical bribery cases

chunk_id: Banking Sector National Risk Assessment (October 2025), Banking Typologies - 4b67d7e36db0f512
body:
- Typology: Human Trafficking & Modern Slavery; Scenario Summary: Multiple individuals, all tied to one business and with the same small residential address, open accounts. CDD reveals all have relocated for work, but branch staff note the group often visits together with an unidentified third party. Concerns arise about potential modern slavery or trafficking.; Key Risk Indicators: ●Unusually high number of unrelated adults at same address ●Accounts opened for salary, daily use ●Group accompanied by unidentified third party
- Typology: Cash Movement to Launder Criminal Proceeds; Scenario Summary: Large sums of Manx currency deposited locally, quickly withdrawn as UK sterling at Isle of Man seaport/airport ATMs, and then carried off-island. The pattern suggests cash movement intended to facilitate laundering and remove illicit funds.; Key Risk Indicators: ●Immediate withdrawal of deposited cash ●Use of ATMs dispensing foreign currency ●Frequent travel coinciding with withdrawals
- Typology: Drug Trafficking Indicators; Scenario Summary: Retail employee's account sees excessive turnover, mostly third-party payments for games consoles and designer goods. Repetitive sales of the same items, frequent outbound transfers, and cash withdrawals at sea terminal ATMs point to possible illicit trade and money laundering.; Key Risk Indicators: ●Excessive account turnover vs. stated income ●Multiple incoming third-party payments ●Cash withdrawals at transport terminals
